land.text: central Chile from Copiapó to the Bío-Bío

predecessors.note: The Captaincy General of Chile; Patria Vieja infobox 'Territories of the Captaincy General of Chile'. The First Junta of 18 September 1810 governed in the king's name; independence was proclaimed on 12 February 1818.

capitals.name: Santiago
capitals.note: 'The capital and largest city is Santiago' (founded 12 February 1541).

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe: Cliopatria begins in 1812 but the Patria Vieja is dated 'between the First Junta of the Government (September 18, 1810) and the Disaster of Rancagua (October 1, 1814)', infobox 1810-1814 and 'Territories of the Captaincy General of Chile'. The 1812 outline is used for 1810-1811; the page names no provinces and gives no area.

225,746 km2 for 1812-1814: Copiapó to the Bío-Bío (Atacama, Coquimbo, Valparaíso, Santiago, O'Higgins, Maule, Ñuble and 47 percent of Bío-Bío by the gazetteer). The infobox of the Patria Vieja gives no area; the Chile page's 756,102 km2 is the modern country. In 1812 the first constitutional decree 'agreed to recognize the king if he accepted certain constitutional regulations'; royalist forces under Pareja came by sea in 1813 and the Treaty of Lircay was signed on 14 May 1814. The outline ends with the Disaster of Rancagua (1-2 October 1814), a year in which Cliopatria still draws it whole.

correction.text: central Chile north of Concepción, held after Chacabuco; 'After Maipú, the royalists retreated to Concepción'

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe, years Cliopatria leaves empty (1815-1819 has no Chile row): 'The resulting Battle of Chacabuco, on February 12, 1817, was a decisive victory for the independence forces', independence was declared on 12 February 1818 and after Maipú (5 April 1818) 'the royalists retreated to Concepción'. The patriots hold central Chile north of the Concepción region; the south (Concepción, Valdivia, Chiloé) is the Spanish Empire's until 1820 and 1826. 1815-1816 stays empty: after the Disaster of Rancagua the Reconquista begins and the page lists no Chilean territory.

247,194 km2 for 1820-1821: 1812 outline plus Valdivia (37 percent of Los Ríos), 18 percent of Los Lagos and 8 percent of Araucanía by the gazetteer. 'In 1820, Cochrane administered a stunning blow to the remaining royalist forces in a successful attack on a complex of fortifications at Valdivia.' The page does not say when Concepción returned to Chile, so that part is unverified: page budget.

293,644 km2 for 1822-1827: +46,000 km2 over 1820, nearly all of it the Atacama coast (Antofagasta region 1 to 34 percent, bbox north from -25.4 to -24.0). No page opened dates or describes a northern boundary before 1879; the Chile page does not discuss it. Unverified: page budget.

correction.text: the 1828 outline, with Chiloé, held from 1826

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe: Cliopatria's 1828 shape (Los Lagos 18 to 33 percent, south edge -41.9 to -43.5) is Chiloé; the page dates it to 1826 ('the last Spanish territory in Chile, the archipelago of Chiloé, was not conquered until 1826, during the government of Ramón Freire'; the Chile page: 'incorporated in 1826'). The 1828 outline is used from 1826.

304,465 km2 for 1828-1865, unchanged for 38 years; no page opened gives a boundary event in that span (the Strait of Magellan was 'controlled by country in 1843' and is in the ledger as a small enclave: Cliopatria does not draw it before 1885).

314,537 km2 for 1866-1879 (+10,000 km2): Bío-Bío rises from 47 to 66 percent and Araucanía from 8 to 13 percent, the Malleco line of the Occupation of Araucanía: Mulchén fort (December 1861 - May 1862), Angol (1862) and a coastal fort between Lebu and the Imperial River (1866). The page gives no area incorporated.

correction.text: shape unchanged: Chile proper plus Tarapacá (ceded 1883), with Tacna, Arica, Moquegua and Lima occupied, not annexed

keyframe_review.note: 428,506 km2 for 1880-1884 (+114,000 km2): Tarapacá, Arica, Tacna, Moquegua, 75 percent of Lima Province and parts of Puno and Ica (by the gazetteer), the land Chilean forces took in the War of the Pacific. Shape unchanged but its status is not annexation: Tarapacá was occupied from November 1879 and ceded by the Treaty of Ancón on 20 October 1883; 'Chile was also to occupy the provinces of Tacna and Arica for 10 years'; Lima was occupied from January 1881 to 29 October 1883 and the last Chilean forces embarked at Callao on 4 August 1884. The shape omits the Bolivian coast (Antofagasta region), which Chile held from 14 February 1879 (the shape of Bolivia keeps it to 1904). The ledger carries all of this as occupations.

correction.text: shape unchanged, with Tacna and Arica occupied (Peruvian sovereignty), the Bolivian coast still outside it

keyframe_review.note: 731,845 km2 for 1885-1904 (+303,000 km2): the Araucanía complete (14 to 98 percent), Los Ríos and Los Lagos whole, Aisén and Magallanes at 95 percent. The Araucanía was 'subjugated' on 1 June 1883; the Boundary Treaty of 23 July 1881 gave Chile the western Tierra del Fuego and the Strait ('Tierra del Fuego ... Chilean on the western side and Argentine on the eastern'); Chile had held the Strait since 1843 (Fuerte Bulnes). No page opened mentions Aisén. Shape unchanged, but Tacna and Arica (49 cells of Peru's Tacna) stay occupied, not annexed, and the Bolivian coast is still occupied rather than inside the outline.

correction.text: shape unchanged, with Tacna and Arica occupied until 1929

keyframe_review.note: 817,411 km2 for 1905-1923, the largest: Antofagasta region to 96 percent and Tarapacá to 95 percent, the Bolivian coast of the 1904 treaty ('signed in Santiago de Chile on 20 October 1904', ratifications exchanged 10 March 1905; 'Chilean sovereignty was recognized by Bolivia over the territory from the ocean'). The infobox of the Chile page gives 756,102 km2 for the modern country (ratio 1.08, within the factor of two; the outline holds about 61,000 km2 more than the land). Shape unchanged, but Tacna and Arica (Peruvian sovereignty) are still occupied until 1929.

correction.text: shape unchanged, with Tacna and Arica occupied

keyframe_review.note: 816,188 km2 for 1924-1925 (-1,223 km2): the page gives no event; the change is about five cells and no page explains it. Tacna and Arica are still occupied (the plebiscite arbitrated by Pershing in 1925 and Lassiter in 1926 'never took place').

correction.text: shape unchanged, Tarata returned, with Tacna and Arica occupied until 1929

keyframe_review.note: 809,341 km2 for 1926-1928 (-6,847 km2): Tacna drops from 84 to 41 percent of its department, the Tarata province, 'the return of Tarata to Peru on September 1, 1925' ('From 1880 to 1925, the province was administered by Chile'). Shape unchanged otherwise; Tacna and Arica are occupied until 1929.

801,914 km2 for 1929-1938 (-7,427 km2): Tacna to Peru. 'The treaty was signed on 3 June 1929 in Lima'; infobox 'Effective: 28 August 1929'; 'Tacna was awarded to Peru' and 'Chile retained its sovereignty over Arica'. The Chile page gives 756,102 km2 for the modern country (ratio 1.06).
803,137 km2 for 1939-1972 (+1,223 km2 over 1929): about five cells, not explained by any page opened. Unverified: page budget.
801,914 km2 for 1973-1989 (-1,223 km2), the same five-cell difference as 1924, no event on the pages opened ('On 11 September 1973, a military coup overthrew Allende' changed no border).
803,137 km2 for 1990 alone ('The regime ended in 1990, following a referendum in 1988'); same outline as 1939-1972.

803,137 km2 for 1991-2023; the Chile page gives 756,102 km2 (ratio 1.06). Chile's Antarctic claim (about 1,250,000 km2, suspended under the Antarctic Treaty; 2,006,360 km2 with it) is not in any shape.

region.text: central Chile from Copiapó to the Bío-Bío

ledger.note: 18 September 1810: Chile forms its First National Junta. The Patria Vieja runs 'between the First Junta of the Government (September 18, 1810) and the Disaster of Rancagua (October 1, 1814)'; a national junta 'was formed on 18 September 1810' (Chile page). Governing in the king's name; independence follows on 12 February 1818. The pages name no provinces; the core is read as the 1812 outline.

region.text: the Concepción region

ledger.note: 1813: the viceroy of Peru sends an army against Chile. 'In 1813, he sent a military expedition by sea under the command of Antonio Pareja to deal with the situation in Chile.' The page gives no landing place; the zone is read as the Concepción region (unverified: page budget). The Treaty of Lircay was signed on 14 May 1814.

region.text: the Concepción region

ledger.note: 1-2 October 1814: the Disaster of Rancagua ends the Patria Vieja. 'The Disaster of Rancagua, on October 1 and 2 of 1814, was fought fiercely'; 'Harassed on all sides, Carrera resigned, in what is commonly taken to mark the beginning of the period of the Reconquista.'

region.text: all the land of the Patria Vieja

ledger.note: October 1814: Spain reconquers Chile. After Rancagua 'the period of the Reconquista' begins and 'Intermittent warfare continued until 1817' (Chile page). The pages give no date for the Spanish entry into Santiago; the whole of the Patria Vieja's land goes back to the Captaincy General.

region.text: central Chile north of Concepción, held after Chacabuco; 'After Maipú, the royalists retreated to Concepción'

ledger.note: 12 February 1817: Chacabuco restores the patriots. 'The resulting Battle of Chacabuco, on February 12, 1817, was a decisive victory for the independence forces.' The page names no territory; central Chile north of Concepción is read from the later royalist retreat to Concepción.

12 February 1818: Chile declares independence. 'On 12 February 1818, Chile was proclaimed an independent republic' (Wars of Independence page: 'A declaration of independence was officially issued by Chile on February 12, 1818').

region.text: the Concepción region

ledger.note: 5 April 1818: Maipú, and the royalists fall back on Concepción. 'Then, on April 5, 1818, San Martín inflicted a decisive defeat on Osorio.' After Maipú 'the royalists retreated to Concepción'; Valdivia fell in 1820 and Chiloé in 1826. The contested zone is read as the Concepción region.

region.text: the Concepción region

ledger.note: 1820: Cochrane takes Valdivia. 'In 1820, Cochrane administered a stunning blow to the remaining royalist forces in a successful attack on a complex of fortifications at Valdivia.' The page does not say when Concepción went back to the patriots; the contest is closed with the fall of Valdivia.

region.text: the fortifications at Valdivia

ledger.note: 1820: Valdivia. 'In 1820, Cochrane ... a successful attack on a complex of fortifications at Valdivia.' Valdivia was 'isolated from Central Chile by hostile Mapuche-controlled territory'; Cliopatria's 1820 shape adds Los Ríos and part of Los Lagos.

region.text: the archipelago of Chiloé

ledger.note: 1826: Chiloé, the last Spanish territory in Chile. 'the last Spanish territory in Chile, the archipelago of Chiloé, was not conquered until 1826, during the government of Ramón Freire'; the Chile page: 'the archipelago of Chiloé was incorporated in 1826'.

region.text: the Strait of Magellan: Fuerte Bulnes 1843, Punta Arenas 1847

ledger.note: 1843: Chile founds Fuerte Bulnes on the Strait of Magellan. 'The Republic of Chile founded Fuerte Bulnes in 1843' and 'later moved that settlement to the site of Punta Arenas in 1847'; the Chile page says the region 'started to be controlled by country in 1843'. A small settlement, not a frontier: the rest of Magallanes is in the ledger from 1881.

region.text: Mulchén and Angol, the Malleco line

ledger.note: December 1861 - May 1862: the Occupation of Araucanía begins at Mulchén. Saavedra 'ordered major Pedro Lagos to advance into the confluence of Mulchén River with Bureo River'; a fort was built on land handed over by the chief Manuel Nampai. 'By 1860 land between Bío-Bío and Malleco River was mostly under control of Chileans.' The Mapuche are no state in Cliopatria.

region.text: Mulchén and Angol, the Malleco line

ledger.note: 1862: Angol. Saavedra 'advanced with a group of 800 soldiers into the remnants of the town of Angol'; the page gives no founding date.

region.text: the coast between Lebu and the Imperial River

ledger.note: 1866: a coastal fort between Lebu and the Imperial River. Saavedra ordered it; the page puts Lebu in 1866, not 1862.

region.text: the Bolivian coast, 'the northern part of the province of Antofagasta and a Pacific littoral'

ledger.note: 14 February 1879: Chile seizes Antofagasta. 'On the day of the planned auction, 200 Chilean soldiers arrived by ship at the port city of Antofagasta and seized it without resistance.' War with Bolivia was declared on 1 March and with Peru on 5 April 1879. Chile holds the Bolivian coast, hatched, until the 1904 treaty.

region.text: the Tarapacá Department

ledger.note: November 1879: the Tarapacá campaign. 'The Campaign of Tarapacá began on November 2, 1879' and Chile 'on 19 November 1879, defeated the Allied troops' at San Francisco and Dolores. Chile holds Tarapacá, hatched, until the Treaty of Ancón.

region.text: Moquegua

ledger.note: 1880: Moquegua. Cliopatria's Chile shape includes 96 percent of Moquegua for 1880-1884 and Peru's shape omits it; none of the pages opened names Moquegua (page silent). The span is bridged to the last Chilean embarkation, 4 August 1884.

region.text: the provinces of Tacna and Arica

ledger.note: 26 May 1880: the Battle of Tacna. 'Bolivia withdrew after the Battle of Tacna, on 26 May 1880.'

region.text: the provinces of Tacna and Arica

ledger.note: 7 June 1880: Arica falls. 'On 7 June, after the Battle of Arica, the last Peruvian bastion in the Tacna Department fell.'

region.text: the provinces of Tacna and Arica

ledger.note: 7 June 1880: Chile holds Tacna and Arica. After Ancón 'Chile was also to occupy the provinces of Tacna and Arica for 10 years' (a plebiscite meant for 1893 never took place; Treaty of Lima page: 'administered by Chile since 1883'). Cliopatria draws them as Chilean land to 1928.

region.text: Lima, Peru's capital

ledger.note: 12 January 1881: the Lima campaign. 'In the afternoon of 12 January 1881, three Chilean formations' moved toward Chorrillos; 'Chilean forces occupied Peru's capital Lima in January 1881.'

region.text: Lima, Peru's capital

ledger.note: January 1881: Lima is taken after Chorrillos and Miraflores.

region.text: Lima, Peru's capital

ledger.note: January 1881: Chile occupies Lima. The Peruvian resistance continues in the Sierra (Campaign of the Breña). Cliopatria's 1880 shape includes 75 percent of Lima Province.

region.text: Tierra del Fuego west of 68°34' W and the Strait of Magellan

ledger.note: 23 July 1881: the Boundary Treaty with Argentina. It 'was signed on 23 July 1881 in Buenos Aires': 'Tierra del Fuego, divided in this manner, shall be Chilean on the western side and Argentine on the eastern' along 68°34' W, and the Straits of Magellan 'neutralized for ever'. Argentina keeps the land east of the Andean divide.

region.admin1: Aisén del General Carlos Ibáñez del Campo
region.text: Chilean Patagonia west of the Andean divide

ledger.note: 1881: Aisén. The treaty runs the line 'over the highest summits of the said Cordilleras which divide the waters'; Cliopatria's 1885 shape holds Aisén at 95 percent but no page opened names it (page silent), so the year is the treaty's, not a Chilean act there.

region.text: the whole Araucanía

ledger.note: 1 June 1883: the Araucanía is 'subjugated'. 'On 1 January 1883, Chile re-founded the old city of Villarrica, ending thus formally the process of occupation of Araucanía'; on 1 June President Santa María declared 'Today the whole Araucanía is subjugated.' Victoria was founded on 28 March 1881 on the Traiguén River; the Mapuche rose on 5 November 1881.

region.text: the Tarapacá Department

ledger.note: 20 October 1883: the Treaty of Ancón. 'Chile and Iglesias's government signed the Peace Treaty of Ancón on 20 October 1883'; 'Peru formally cedes the Tarapacá Department to Chile' (infobox).

region.text: the Tarapacá Department

ledger.note: 20 October 1883: the Treaty of Ancón ends the occupation of Tarapacá by cession.

region.text: Lima, Peru's capital

ledger.note: 29 October 1883: the Chilean occupation of Lima ends. 'On 29 October 1883, the Chilean occupation of Lima ended.'

region.text: Moquegua

ledger.note: 4 August 1884: the Chilean Expeditionary Forces embark at Callao. 'On 4 August 1884, Lynch and the rest of the Chilean Expeditionary Forces embarked in Callao.' The date closes the Moquegua span of 1880-1884 (page silent on Moquegua). On 4 April 1884 Bolivia had signed the truce at Valparaíso, accepting Chilean administration of its coast.

region.text: Easter Island

ledger.note: 9 September 1888: Chile takes possession of Easter Island. 'On 9 September 1888, Chile took possession of Easter Island.' Cliopatria's shapes do not include it.

region.text: the Bolivian coast, 'the northern part of the province of Antofagasta and a Pacific littoral'

ledger.note: 20 October 1904: Bolivia cedes its coast. The Treaty of Peace and Friendship 'was signed in Santiago de Chile on 20 October 1904'; 'Chilean sovereignty was recognized by Bolivia over the territory from the ocean' (96 boundary points from Cerro Zapaleri to Cerro Chipapa); ratifications exchanged at La Paz on 10 March 1905. Cliopatria's Bolivia row loses the coast in 1905.

region.text: the Bolivian coast, 'the northern part of the province of Antofagasta and a Pacific littoral'

ledger.note: 20 October 1904: the occupation of the Bolivian coast ends in annexation.

region.text: the Tarata province (the land in the 1925 shape and not in the 1926 shape)

ledger.note: 1 September 1925: Tarata returns to Peru. 'From 1880 to 1925, the province was administered by Chile'; 'the return of Tarata to Peru on September 1, 1925'. President Coolidge's mediation 'was significant in the conclusion of the 42-year dispute'. The region is the land in the 1925 shape and not in the 1926 shape.

region.text: the provinces of Tacna and Arica

ledger.note: 28 August 1929: the Tacna-Arica occupation ends. 'The treaty was signed on 3 June 1929 in Lima'; infobox 'Effective: 28 August 1929'. A plebiscite meant for 1893 was never held.

region.text: Tacna, 'awarded to Peru' (the land in the 1928 shape and not in the 1929 shape)

ledger.note: 28 August 1929: Tacna goes to Peru. 'Tacna was awarded to Peru'; Chile also agreed to pay up to US$6 million in compensation.

region.text: Arica, over which 'Chile retained its sovereignty'

ledger.note: 28 August 1929: Arica stays with Chile. 'Chile retained its sovereignty over Arica.'

wars.name: Chilean War of Independence
wars.outcome: The patriots lost at Rancagua (1-2 October 1814), won at Chacabuco (12 February 1817) and Maipú (5 April 1818), proclaimed independence on 12 February 1818, took Valdivia in 1820 and Chiloé in 1826.
wars.note: The page dates the Treaty of Lircay 14 May 1814.

wars.name: War of the Pacific

zones.text: the Bolivian coast, 'the northern part of the province of Antofagasta and a Pacific littoral'
the provinces of Tacna and Arica

wars.outcome: Chile seized Antofagasta on 14 February 1879, took Tarapacá, Tacna, Arica and Lima, and gained Tarapacá by the Treaty of Ancón (20 October 1883); Bolivia signed a truce at Valparaíso on 4 April 1884 and ceded its coast in 1904.
wars.note: Declarations: Bolivia 1 March 1879, Peru 5 April 1879. Moquegua is not on the page.

wars.name: Occupation of Araucanía
wars.outcome: Chile advanced from the Bío-Bío and Malleco line (Mulchén 1861-62, Angol 1862, a coastal fort in 1866), founded Victoria (28 March 1881), put down the Mapuche rising of 5 November 1881 and re-founded Villarrica (1 January 1883); on 1 June 1883 'the whole Araucanía is subjugated'.

wars.name: Tacna-Arica dispute

zones.text: the provinces of Tacna and Arica

wars.outcome: Chile administered Tacna and Arica from 1880/1883; a plebiscite meant for 1893 never took place; Tarata returned to Peru on 1 September 1925; the Treaty of Lima (3 June 1929, effective 28 August) awarded Tacna to Peru and left Arica to Chile.

wars.name: Patagonian boundary dispute with Argentina

zones.text: Tierra del Fuego west of 68°34' W and the Strait of Magellan

wars.outcome: The Boundary Treaty of 23 July 1881 divided Tierra del Fuego at 68°34' W and neutralised the Strait; 'In 1902, war was again avoided when King Edward VII of Britain agreed to mediate'; the Puna de Atacama was settled in 1899.
wars.note: No fighting; listed because the page records war being averted twice.

certainty.note: Unsurveyed frontiers: the Mapuche Araucanía until 1883, the Atacama desert and the Andes; the 1822 northern limit is not on any page.

The treaty line with Argentina (23 July 1881) runs 'over the highest summits of the said Cordilleras which divide the waters' and was fixed in the field only by the 1902 arbitration; the Bolivian coast and Tacna-Arica were occupied, not bounded.
The 1904 treaty delimits the Bolivian boundary through 96 points; the 1929 Treaty of Lima fixes Peru's; the 1902 award and the 1881 treaty fix Argentina's. The Antarctic claim is excluded.

notes: Cliopatria's Republic of Chile row has a gap 1815-1819 (the Reconquista and the patriots' return): a new keyframe covers 1817-1819 and 1815-1816 stay empty, with a 'loss' in 1814 and a 'gain' in 1817; the first shape is 1812 (the first constitutional decree) though the First Junta is 18 September 1810, so 1810-1811 get a new keyframe. 1826 (Chiloé) gets a new keyframe because Cliopatria starts its Chiloé outline in 1828. Status corrections: the 1880-1928 outlines treat Tacna, Arica (to 1929), Tarapacá (to 1883), Lima (1881-1883) and Moquegua as Chilean land; the pages say they were occupied, so the ledger records occupations (hatched) and the verdicts leave the outline as drawn. The Bolivian coast (Antofagasta region minus the pre-1879 Chilean south) is occupied from 14 February 1879 but is Bolivia's in Cliopatria until 1904; the Chile outline takes it in 1905. Not settled: the date of Chile's northern limit in 1822 (+46,000 km2, the Atacama coast); when Concepción returned to the patriots; Aisén (no page); the Moquegua occupation (page silent, bridged at confidence 1); the five-cell differences of 1924, 1939, 1973 and 1990. Pages that would not load: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tacna%E2%80%93Arica_compromise, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tacna%E2%80%93Arica_dispute and https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tacna_and_Arica_Question (not found; the Treaty of Lima (1929) page was used instead). Needs dossiers: the Mapuche of the Araucanía (independent until 1883; Cliopatria has no row; slug mapuche); the war counterparts bolivia and republic-of-peru are in group am-08. Gazetteer lacks Mulchén (replaced by Angol), Tarata, Chiloé, Easter Island and Juan Fernández. Antarctica (Chilean claim) is outside every shape; Easter Island (9 September 1888) is in the ledger only.
